_what_this_is: The last time anyone checked whether upstream moved. Distinct from upstream-review.json, which records the versions a human has REVIEWED. This file records only that a LOOK happened, and what it saw.
_why_it_exists: Every dependency floats to latest at build time, and the marker test in upstream-review.json fires when a build happens -- but nothing makes a build happen. Releases are manual, so a quiet month is a month in which upstream can move unobserved. The marker catches 'we are about to ship a version nobody reviewed'; this catches 'upstream moved while nobody was looking'.
_why_this_is_enough: A scheduled CI poller was the obvious answer and is not needed here. This project is built entirely through an agent, so a directive in CLAUDE.md runs on every working session by construction -- the check happens because work happens. Dependabot cannot do this job anyway: verified 2026-08-14 against dependabot-core's own test table, a NuGet Version="*" is rewritten to "*" and produces no PR, and npm "latest" is skipped by a dist-tag guard. Dependabot bumps declared floors, and this project declares none.
_how_to_resolve: Resolve each upstream the way the BUILD resolves it, not the way a registry query defaults. In particular playwright-core is NOT npm 'latest' -- it arrives as @playwright/mcp's own exact dependency. On 2026-08-15 npm 'latest' for playwright-core was 1.62.1 while the version that actually ships is 1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-05, because upstream publishes daily alphas and pins one exactly. Checking 'latest' would have reported drift that does not exist, in the safe direction today and the unsafe direction tomorrow.
_honesty_rule: Only stamp lastChecked after a lookup actually returned a version. A date written from intent rather than from a result is worse than no date, because it reads identically to a real one and silences the next check for a day.
result: Checked 2026-09-15. DRIFT on two of the five, and it is the same pair that moved yesterday. @playwright/mcp 0.0.80 -> 0.0.81, published 2026-09-14T21:25:54Z -- about two hours after the review that adopted 0.0.80 was written -- carrying playwright-core 1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-31 -> 1.64.0-alpha-2026-09-14 as ONE resolution read out of that version's own dependencies. That is a MINOR line move rather than another daily alpha of the same one, so it is a wider door than the last roll was. NOTHING WAS ADOPTED, and the three places that name a version agree: the payload is 0.0.80, upstream-review.json records 0.0.80, and tool-verdicts.json's judgedAgainst was moved to 0.0.80 in the same batch as this check. Closing it is UPSTREAM-REVIEW.md again, plus the re-verification rows a playwright-core move puts in play. The trap _how_to_resolve exists for fired again and in a THIRD shape: npm 'latest' for playwright-core read 1.63.0 on this date, a stable release that is now BEHIND the alpha that actually ships (1.63.0 < 1.64.0-alpha-2026-09-14), where on 2026-09-14 it was ahead and on 2026-08-15 behind. The 'next' dist-tag happened to read 1.64.0-alpha-2026-09-14, the same string as the pin, which is a coincidence of the day and not a second way to resolve it. It was read out of the dependency, as the table says. Previous result, 2026-09-14: Checked 2026-09-14, and the drift found that morning was REVIEWED AND CLOSED the same day. Corrected 2026-09-14 (previously "DRIFT on three of the five, unreviewed and unbumped; ... NOTHING WAS BUMPED and upstream-review.json was not touched: three upstreams are now unreviewed, and closing them is UPSTREAM-REVIEW.md plus the re-verification rows a playwright-core move puts in play") -- that sentence described the state before the review, and it is replaced rather than deleted so a reader who met it learns how it was closed. WHAT THE CHECK SAW: @playwright/mcp 0.0.79 -> 0.0.80 (dist-tag latest, published 2026-09-01), carrying playwright-core 1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-05 -> 1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-31 as ONE resolution read out of that version's own dependencies; node v24.20.0 -> v24.21.0 (Krypton, openssl 3.5.7 -> 3.5.8 the only component change, security:false). The trap _how_to_resolve exists for fired in the UNSAFE direction: npm 'latest' for playwright-core read 1.63.0 on this date, a STABLE release and newer by SemVer than the alpha that actually ships, so reporting it would have looked entirely legitimate rather than obviously odd. It was not taken. ModelContextProtocol 2.2.0 and Velopack 1.2.0 were re-read from nuget.org stable and are unmoved, and the vendored SQLite row was read in the same pass from sqlite.org's machine-readable PRODUCT line and is unmoved to the byte. HOW IT WAS CLOSED: UPSTREAM-REVIEW.md was followed end to end. The payload was rebuilt through the build's own resolver, all four golden snapshots were regenerated and diffed, the two that moved were adjudicated, and upstream-review.json now records 0.0.80 / 1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-31 / v24.21.0 with what was adopted, what was declined and why, and every re-verification row answered by name. THE REVIEW IS DONE AND THE ADOPTION IS NOT FINISHED, and those are two files by design: the roll added TWO TOOLS -- browser_start_recording and browser_stop_recording -- and a verdict is a human judgement about this product rather than a record of upstream, so tool-verdicts.json was left untouched, judgedAgainst included, and the suite is red on exactly that one pending decision. Two upstream BEHAVIOUR changes were found that no snapshot could have shown: the chromiumSandbox config key is now honoured (microsoft/playwright#42288 arrived; BrowserAI is unaffected because it passes --sandbox on the command line), and scaleImageToFitMessage has been DELETED, so an inline screenshot is no longer downscaled to 1568 px or re-encoded -- measured as byte-identical to the file at 1920x1080. That second one makes a sentence in the model-facing server instructions false and is a product decision, reported rather than taken. FOUND WHILE LOOKING, AND NOT ONE OF THE FIVE, now also closed: src/BrowserAI/packages.lock.json carried an uncommitted re-resolve nobody asked for. It was reset to HEAD and redone as the build's own two-step -- `dotnet restore --force-evaluate` then `--locked-mode`, exit 0 -- which moved ALL THREE lock files rather than the one the rogue restore had touched. Microsoft.Extensions / ILCompiler / ILLink 10.0.11 -> 10.0.12, MinVer 7.0.0 -> 8.0.0, and in the test projects TUnit 1.65.68 -> 1.67.0, Microsoft.Testing.Platform 2.3.3 -> 2.4.0 and CsWin32 0.3.321 -> 0.3.333. Neither MinVer nor the test stack is a reviewed upstream, so no marker test gates any of them. MinVer 8.0.0's single breaking change is that MinVerDefaultPreReleasePhase now hard-errors instead of warning; this tree sets only MinVerTagPrefix and no such variable exists in it, MinVer.Lib's derivation source is byte-identical between 7.0.0 and 8.0.0, and the derived string is unchanged in shape -- `git describe --tags --long` v1.0.0-206-g5f12649, MinVerVersion 1.0.1-alpha.0.206. global.json's _provenance was corrected in the same pass: it named 10.0.302 as the SDK installed on this machine, and `dotnet --list-sdks` reports 10.0.401 and nothing else. The FLOOR was deliberately not raised. Previous result, 2026-08-30: no drift, on any of the five, and none on the vendored pin either. All five resolved the way the build resolves them and came back identical to upstream-review.json: @playwright/mcp dist-tag latest 0.0.79; playwright-core 1.63.0-alpha-2026-08-05 read out of THAT version's own dependencies rather than from npm latest; ModelContextProtocol 2.2.0 and Velopack 1.2.0 from nuget.org stable, published 2026-08-13 and 2026-06-04; node v24.20.0, still the newest entry with an lts field (Krypton, released 2026-08-26, npm 11.19.0, v8 13.6.233.17, openssl 3.5.7, security false), with the Current line at v26.8.1 and deliberately not tracked. This is the check taken on the day the release candidate was finished, so it is also the last look before the cut. Result before that, kept because it is how the previous drift was closed: node moved v24.19.0 -> v24.20.0 and the move was REVIEWED and ADOPTED the same day, 2026-08-27, by the same procedure this entry records.

_why_vendored_is_a_separate_section: `resolved` above is the five upstreams the BUILD floats to latest, and UpstreamReviewTests.TheFiveReviewedUpstreamsAreTheOnesTheDriftCheckResolves holds that set identical, in both directions, to upstream-review.json's. `vendored` below is source PINNED inside this tree: it does not float, no build resolves it, it has no golden snapshot to diff, and reviewing it is a human downloading one zip and re-running the gate. Putting it in `resolved` would either break that correspondence or force a name into upstream-review.json that no review procedure applies to -- and editing upstream-review.json to make a test pass is exactly what CLAUDE.md forbids. So a pin is never counted as a float, and the row below carries its own `checked` date because the top-level `lastChecked` is about the five.

sqlite-amalgamation.vendored_at: third-party/sqlite/sqlite3.c and third-party/sqlite/sqlite3.h, extracted from sqlite-amalgamation-3530400.zip. shell.c and sqlite3ext.h are NOT vendored: nothing here builds a shell, and sqlite3ext.h is already inlined into the amalgamation.

archive.name: sqlite-amalgamation-3530400.zip
archive.note: sqlite.org publishes SHA3-256 and not SHA-256. Verified 2026-08-26: the downloaded archive hashed to exactly this value, and the size matched to the byte. The archive itself is NOT in the tree, so nothing can re-derive this hash -- it is provenance. What IS re-derivable is the pair of file hashes below, and SqliteTests checks them on every run.

files.note: SHA-256 of the files as they sit on disk. Stable across checkouts because .gitattributes normalises everything to LF and the amalgamation already ships LF (measured 2026-08-26: 269,649 LF and zero CR in sqlite3.c), so git rewrites nothing on the way in or out.

sqlite-amalgamation.how: sqlite.org/download.html, and read the MACHINE-READABLE line rather than the rendered table: the page source carries `PRODUCT,<version>,<year>/sqlite-amalgamation-<n>.zip,<bytes>,<sha3-256>` for exactly this artifact. Download that URL, check the SHA3-256 BEFORE unzipping, and take sqlite3.c and sqlite3.h. This is NOT a registry query and NOT an npm or nuget `latest`: no maintained package carries this source at all, which is why it is pinned here. The cross-check is the floating `SourceGear.sqlite3` nuget version, whose version number IS the SQLite version and which lags sqlite.org by 3-30 days -- and since 2026-08-26 it costs nothing to read, because the test project references it (it is what puts an e_sqlite3.dll beside a CoreCLR test host) so every re-resolve writes today's SQLite into tests/BrowserAI.Tests/packages.lock.json. A gap between that number and `pinned` above is a prompt to look, never a defect on its own: the package skips some releases.
sqlite-amalgamation.watch: ericsink/SQLitePCL.raw issue 657, 'Provide static libraries for Native AOT deployment' -- open since 2025-12-27, owner said 2026-01-08 he plans to work on it. The 3.x line already ships libe_sqlite3.a for fourteen Linux RIDs and nothing for win-*. THE DAY a win-x64 e_sqlite3.lib ships inside SourceGear.sqlite3, build/Sqlite.targets' compile step is deleted, <NativeLibrary> points into the restored package, and the native floats again like everything else. Check it by globbing the restored package for a .lib under runtimes/win-x64 -- a glob for *.a in the same package returns twenty, which is the positive control that the glob shape works.
